title: When to use illustration instead of photography
excerpt: Illustrate a system or a feeling you cannot photograph honestly. Use photography when the object or the place is the proof a buyer needs to see.
alt: A close view of a smartphone home screen filled with app icons on a pale table. The grid of icons fits a piece about choosing a drawing when a photograph cannot explain the product.
caption: Some products are a system, and a system is hard to photograph. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should a brand use illustration?
faqs.answer: Use it when you are explaining a system, a sequence, or a feeling you cannot photograph without faking the scene. A diagram of how an onboarding flow works, or a drawing of an abstract product, can be clearer than a stock photo of a laptop. The illustration still has to match the voice of the site. A cute style on a serious offer will be read as a mismatch.

faqs.question: When is photography the better proof?
faqs.answer: When the object, the place, or the person is the evidence. A store, a material, a room, a finished piece of work: people want to see the real thing. Google's helpful-content guidance treats photographs as one way to show that the work was actually done. A drawing of a product you could have photographed looks like you had something to hide.

faqs.question: Can a site use both?
faqs.answer: Yes, if each has a job and they share a palette and a level of finish. Photography for proof, illustration for explanation, icons as a quiet third system. If they collide in the same hero, the page looks undecided. Pick one mode for the first screen, and let the other mode support a later section.

markdown:
Use a photograph when the object or the place is the proof. Use an illustration when you are explaining a system, or a feeling you cannot photograph honestly. That is the illustration vs photography brand decision. It is a content decision before it is a style decision.

A buyer can tell the difference between evidence and decoration. Evidence is a picture of the thing you sell, the place you work, or the result you produced. Decoration is a generic scene that could sit on any company's homepage. Decoration is what teams reach for when they have not decided which of the two jobs the image has.

## Photography when the thing is real

If a person could visit, hold, or recognize the subject, photograph it. Materials, food, a shop floor, a finished object, a room, a face you have permission to show. The details that persuade are the details a drawing usually smooths away: the edge of a seam, the color of a glaze, the scale of a space.

Google's guidance on people-first content makes the same point in the context of trust. When you describe how something was done, evidence of the work, including photographs, helps a reader believe the account. A product page or a project page is that kind of account. A photograph of the real result is doing a job a paragraph cannot finish.

Down the Cove is a store. The merchandise and the way it is presented are the proof. A heritage project such as Thomas Bewick has a real body of work and a real history to show. In both cases a photograph, or a faithful reproduction of the work itself, is the honest picture. An illustration that "captures the spirit" of a product you could have shown is a step away from the buyer.

Take the pictures you can stand behind. Permission, accurate color, and a crop that does not invent a scale. A tiny object shot to look monumental will bounce back as a return, or as a loss of trust, the moment it arrives. The photograph's job is to reduce surprise, not to create it.

Stock photography of strangers in glass offices fails this test even when the file is technically fine. The people are not your team. The room is not your room. A careful buyer has seen that image on other sites. It does not prove you exist. If you cannot photograph the real subject yet, use type and a clear interface, or commission a drawing that does not pretend to be a document.

## Illustration when you are explaining

Some products have no honest photograph. A workflow, a protocol, a financial relationship, a piece of software that looks like a form until you understand the sequence. A camera pointed at a laptop will produce a picture of a laptop. It will not produce an explanation.

Draw the system. A small number of steps, real labels, the same words you use in the interface. The drawing should teach one idea. If it needs a legend the size of the drawing, it is a specification leaked onto the homepage. Split it. The homepage gets the simple version. The docs get the full one.

Feelings belong here only when a photograph would be a lie. "Relief when the migration is done" is not a scene you can stage without actors and a fake office. A restrained illustration can stand for the feeling if the surrounding sentence does the explaining. The drawing is not a substitute for the claim. "We move the store without a week of broken checkout" still has to be a sentence. The picture can support it.

Style follows the job. A technical explanation wants consistent strokes, limited color, and type you can read. A feeling wants a narrower range than a children's book, unless that is truly the brand. Pick a palette from the brand's colors so the drawing sits on the site instead of arriving as a guest. Illustrator is a natural place to build that system. The site then uses the exports the way it uses any other asset: sized, named, and versioned.

Do not illustrate a face you could have photographed and pass it off as the founder. Do not draw the customer's logo. Do not invent a product UI that is slicker than the one you ship. The drawing should be simpler than the product, not a fantasy of it. Fantasy is what people remember when the real screen loads.

## One mode on the first screen

The hero should pick a side. A photograph of the product, or an illustration of the system, or the interface itself. Two modes in one hero, a photo with cartoon characters floating on it, splits the claim. The visitor has to decide what kind of company this is before they can decide what you do.

Below the fold you can change modes if the job changes. A project page can open with a photograph of the finished work and later show a diagram of the structure. An article can be mostly text, with a figure where the paragraph would otherwise become a list of arrows. The change should feel intended. A different illustrator on every section, or a mix of three stock styles, feels scraped together.

Icons are a third system, smaller and quieter. They should not compete with the illustration style, and they should not be tiny photographs. Give them their own rules. One stroke, one weight, one grid. If the icons are playful and the product illustrations are severe, the header and the hero argue. Settle it in the brand files before you design the page.

Motion does not decide the mode. A photograph can be still. An illustration can be still. If you animate, animate one idea, and ship a reduced-motion version that keeps the explanation. A drawing that only makes sense while it moves will fail the moment someone pauses it, and some people will pause it because the motion makes them ill.

## What to brief, and what to reject

Write the job in the brief before you write the style. "Explain the three steps of booking, in our words, for a buyer who has never seen the product." Or "show the material at a scale a person can trust, in daylight, with the true color." A brief that only says "make it premium" will come back as a dark photograph of a desk. You will have spent the round and you will still not have proof or an explanation.

Reject images that could be swapped with a competitor's without anyone noticing. Reject illustrations that hide a weak sentence. Reject photographs of the product that you would not let a picky customer inspect. Ask, every time, whether a skeptical buyer would feel informed or managed.

Keep a small library, not a dump. A dozen photographs with a consistent light, or a dozen illustrations with a consistent hand, will outlast a folder of one-off experiments. Name the files for the content, not for the campaign of the month. When the offer changes, you should be able to find the picture that belongs to the new page.

On the site, the image pipeline from the engineering side still applies. An illustration exported at poster size is as rude to a slow connection as a careless photograph. Match the slot. Write alt text that says what the drawing shows. "Diagram of the three booking steps" is useful. "Brand illustration" is not.

## A small set you can actually maintain

Decide how many pictures the site needs this season, then stop. A homepage, a handful of project covers, and one explanatory diagram will do more than a library nobody updates. Each new picture should replace a weaker one or fill a page that is still using a placeholder. Adding files without a slot is how the style splits.

Name the owner. Someone has to say no to the next stock download. On a small team that person is often the founder until a designer is in the work every week. Write the rule where the files live, next to two approved examples. The rule can be four lines: photograph the real object, draw the system, do not mix them in the hero, do not use a scene you do not have rights to keep.

Revisit the set when the offer changes. A diagram of last year's steps, drawn with care, will keep explaining the wrong product with great confidence. Photography goes stale when the product changes color or the shop moves. Schedule a pass. A quiet library that matches the current offer is the whole point of choosing a mode in the first place.

## A review you can do with the page muted

Turn off your memory of the project and look at the homepage for five seconds. What is being proven? If the answer is "someone owns a laptop," the photograph is not doing a job. If the answer is "this is the object" or "this is how it works," the mode is right. Then check the next section. If it repeats the same idea in the other mode, cut one.

Ask who took the photograph or who made the drawing, and whether you can use it a year from now. Rights are part of the choice. A beautiful image you cannot keep is a launch-day liability. Commission the work you need, or photograph it yourself, rather than building the identity on a rental you will have to strip out later.

Put the chosen mode in the brand notes in a few lines. Future pages will drift toward whatever is easiest to download. A written rule, with two examples of yes and one of no, is enough to hold the line. The client portal is a reasonable home for those files and that note once the system exists. The rule should be short enough that someone will actually open it.

[Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) is a place to see public projects where the picture has to match the kind of product it is, from a store to a heritage site. The mode is different because the proof is different.

Icons are the small cousins of this choice, and they go wrong in a header faster than a hero does. [Icon sets that stay quiet](/blog/icon-sets-that-stay-quiet) is the next piece, on keeping one stroke and one weight so the interface does not look assembled from downloads.
